remotes.summary: Remotes are named URLs, and remote-tracking branches like origin/main are your local cache of where the remote's branches were at your last fetch. Fetch downloads, pull integrates, push uploads, and tags travel only when you ask.
points: `git fetch` updates `origin/*` refs only; your branches, index and files never change. `git pull` is fetch plus merge (or rebase).
Remote-tracking refs change only on fetch, pull or push, so `git status` ahead/behind counts are as stale as your last fetch.
A push must be a fast-forward of the remote branch; "rejected (fetch first)" means someone pushed first, so fetch and integrate before pushing again.
With `push.default = simple`, a branch without an upstream needs `git push -u origin <branch>`, or set `push.autoSetupRemote = true`.
Tags are not pushed by default: use `git push origin <tag>`, `--follow-tags` (annotated, reachable) or `--tags` (all). `git describe` uses annotated tags unless you pass `--tags`.
Deleted remote branches linger locally until `git fetch --prune`; tags need `--prune-tags`.
`--depth` implies `--single-branch`; partial clones (`--filter=blob:none`) keep full history and fetch file contents on demand.
traps: A plain `git fetch` never moves a tag you already have; moving a published tag silently leaves teammates on the old commit.
On Windows, Git for Windows' system config sets `pull.rebase = false`, so `git pull` merges where a clean Linux Git would stop and ask.
Fork pull requests don't get repository secrets in `pull_request` workflows, and `GITHUB_TOKEN` is read-only.
